---
title: "Project resources"
subtitle: "Declaring additional files for the rendered output"
---

A Quarto project's published output usually contains more than just
the rendered `.html` files. Datasets, downloadable extras, images
referenced from JavaScript, copies of canonical sources, redirect
pages — none of these go through the document pipeline, but they
all need to land in `_site/` (or wherever the project's `output-dir`
points) and be included when you run `quarto publish`.

The **`resources:`** field tells Quarto to copy specific files into
the output directory verbatim. Three independent ways to declare a
resource — author YAML, engines, and Lua filters — all converge
into a single per-project list before files are copied.

## Declaring resources in YAML

### Project-level: `_quarto.yml`

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  resources:
    - data/*.csv         # globs are supported
    - extras/notes.txt
    - downloads/handbook.pdf
```

Project-level resources are resolved relative to the project root,
and each matched file is copied to the same relative path under
`output-dir`. So `data/q1.csv` lands at `_site/data/q1.csv`.

A single string is accepted as shorthand for a one-element list:

```yaml
project:
  resources: extras/notes.txt
```

### Document-level: YAML frontmatter

A document can declare resources in its own frontmatter:

```yaml
---
title: "Quarterly Report"
resources:
  - data/q1-2026.csv
  - figures/raw/baseline.png
---
```

Document-level resources resolve relative to the **document's
parent directory**, so a doc at `posts/foo.qmd` declaring
`data/q1.csv` reads from `posts/data/q1.csv` and writes to
`_site/posts/data/q1.csv`.

## Engine-emitted resources

Render engines (knitr, jupyter, future engines) often produce
supporting files — figure images, generated CSVs, intermediate
data. Quarto picks these up automatically through
`ExecuteResult.supporting_files` and routes them through the same
publishing pipeline as author-declared resources. No extra
configuration is needed; if your knitr chunk produces
`doc_files/figure-html/cell-1.png`, that file lands in
`_site/doc_files/figure-html/cell-1.png` and is included in
`quarto publish`.

## Adding resources from a Lua filter

User Lua filters can register a file as a published resource by
calling `quarto.doc.add_resource(path)`:

```lua
function Image(img)
  -- After rewriting an Image's src to point at a generated thumbnail,
  -- make sure the thumbnail itself ships with the site.
  quarto.doc.add_resource("thumbs/" .. img.src)
  return img
end
```

The path is interpreted relative to the document being processed.
A `camelCase` alias `quarto.doc.addResource(path)` is provided for
parity with Pandoc filter conventions.

## Rules and constraints

- **Globs are author-only.** Engine and Lua-filter contributions
  must be exact paths. (Engines and filters know what they
  produced; we'd rather not have them re-discover it via globs.)
- **Out-of-project paths are an error.** A resource that resolves
  outside the project root produces a clear render-time error
  rather than silent surprising behavior. If you genuinely need to
  publish content from outside the project, copy it in (a build
  script, a `before-render` hook, or simply a symlink) and
  declare it from inside.
- **Author declarations are irrevocable.** Engines and Lua filters
  can *add* to the resource list but cannot remove what the YAML
  declared. Even if a filter mutates the post-filter
  `meta.resources` to drop an entry, the author's declaration
  still ships. (See the design notes for why: static analysis of a
  project's resource set must be tractable without running the
  pipeline.)
- **Negative globs (`!internal/*`) are not supported in v1.** If
  you need them, file an issue describing the use case and
  expected semantics.

## How `quarto publish` picks up resources

After every project render, Quarto writes
`<project>/.quarto/render-manifest.json` listing every rendered
file plus every resolved resource (with `origin` metadata for
diagnostics). `quarto publish` reads this manifest and ships
everything in it. If the manifest is missing — for example when
publishing the output of an older Quarto version — `publish`
falls back to walking the output directory.

You normally never look at the manifest directly, but its presence
means publishing is reproducible: the file set is the one your
render computed, not whatever happened to be on disk afterwards.
